XIANG-L-31-05.essay: Steadfastness removes regret because influence has not brought harm. Restless thoughts, however, cannot accomplish something broad.

XIANG-L-31-06.label: 31 咸 小象 5
XIANG-L-31-06.essay: Influence felt in the back shows that the aspiration has reached only an outer or limited part of the person.

XIANG-L-31-07.label: 31 咸 小象 6
XIANG-L-31-07.essay: Influence confined to jaw, cheeks, and tongue is little more than persuasive speech, not deep or lasting feeling.

XIANG-L-32-01.label: 32 恆 大象
XIANG-L-32-01.original: 雷風，恆；君子以立不易方。
XIANG-L-32-01.essay: Thunder and wind operate together in Constancy. The exemplary person establishes a firm direction and does not casually abandon it.

XIANG-L-32-02.label: 32 恆 小象 1
XIANG-L-32-02.essay: Seeking excessive depth or permanence from the outset invites misfortune; durability must develop over time.

XIANG-L-32-03.label: 32 恆 小象 2
XIANG-L-32-03.essay: The second line loses regret because it can sustain a balanced course for a long time.

XIANG-L-32-04.label: 32 恆 小象 3
XIANG-L-32-04.essay: When a person cannot maintain virtue consistently, there is no secure place for that person to be accepted.

XIANG-L-32-05.label: 32 恆 小象 4
XIANG-L-32-05.essay: Remaining a long time in an unsuitable position cannot produce the game sought in the hunt.

XIANG-L-32-06.label: 32 恆 小象 5
XIANG-L-32-06.original: 婦人貞吉，從一而終也。夫子制義，從婦凶也。
XIANG-L-32-06.essay: The text praises a wife's constancy within ancient marital roles, while warning that a husband must judge duty himself; this reflects historical role expectations.

XIANG-L-32-07.label: 32 恆 小象 6
XIANG-L-32-07.essay: Agitated persistence at the highest place achieves little. Restlessness is the opposite of genuine constancy.

XIANG-L-33-01.label: 33 遯 大象
XIANG-L-33-01.original: 天下有山，遯；君子以遠小人，不惡而嚴。
XIANG-L-33-01.essay: A mountain stands beneath Heaven, depicting Retreat. The exemplary person keeps distance from unworthy influences without hatred, while maintaining dignity.

XIANG-L-33-02.label: 33 遯 小象 1
XIANG-L-33-02.essay: Retreating last is dangerous; if one refrains from going forward, the danger need not arise.

XIANG-L-33-03.label: 33 遯 小象 2
XIANG-L-33-03.essay: The yellow oxhide signifies a determination bound so firmly that it cannot easily be loosened.

XIANG-L-33-04.label: 33 遯 小象 3
XIANG-L-33-04.original: 系遯之厲，有疾憊也。畜臣妾吉，不可大事也。
XIANG-L-33-04.essay: Retreat entangled by attachments brings weakness and distress. Managing minor household affairs is possible, but great undertakings are inappropriate.

XIANG-L-33-05.label: 33 遯 小象 4
XIANG-L-33-05.essay: An exemplary person can choose a graceful retreat, whereas a petty person finds such withdrawal difficult.

XIANG-L-33-06.label: 33 遯 小象 5
XIANG-L-33-06.essay: Timely and worthy retreat is fortunate because it sets the intention right.

XIANG-L-33-07.label: 33 遯 小象 6
XIANG-L-33-07.essay: A generous and unencumbered retreat encounters no disadvantage because nothing remains to cause doubt.

XIANG-L-34-01.label: 34 大壯 大象
XIANG-L-34-01.original: 雷在天上，大壯；君子以非禮弗履。
XIANG-L-34-01.essay: Thunder resounds in Heaven in Great Strength. The exemplary person refuses to take any step contrary to proper conduct.

XIANG-L-34-02.label: 34 大壯 小象 1
XIANG-L-34-02.essay: Strength expressed only in the toes soon reaches its limit. Bold movement without judgment cannot last.

XIANG-L-34-03.label: 34 大壯 小象 2
XIANG-L-34-03.essay: The second line is fortunate through constancy because it occupies a balanced position.

XIANG-L-34-04.label: 34 大壯 小象 3
XIANG-L-34-04.essay: A petty person uses brute strength; the exemplary person declines to act that way.

XIANG-L-34-05.label: 34 大壯 小象 4
XIANG-L-34-05.essay: The fence breaks and the ram's horns are freed; obstacles have opened, making continued advancement possible.

XIANG-L-34-06.label: 34 大壯 小象 5
XIANG-L-34-06.essay: Losing the ram results from occupying an unsuitable position, not simply from a shortage of force.

XIANG-L-34-07.label: 34 大壯 小象 6
XIANG-L-34-07.original: 不能退，不能遂，不詳也。艱則吉，咎不長也。
XIANG-L-34-07.essay: Unable either to retreat or to advance, the ram faces a grave impasse. Patient endurance can keep blame from continuing.

XIANG-L-35-01.label: 35 晉 大象
XIANG-L-35-01.original: 明出地上，晉；君子以自昭明德。
XIANG-L-35-01.essay: Light rises above Earth in Progress. The exemplary person makes personal virtue increasingly bright and visible.

XIANG-L-35-02.label: 35 晉 小象 1
XIANG-L-35-02.original: 晉如，摧如；獨行正也。裕无咎；未受命也。
XIANG-L-35-02.essay: Progress initially meets resistance, yet upright solitary conduct remains valid. Being patient before receiving a mandate avoids blame.

XIANG-L-35-03.label: 35 晉 小象 2
XIANG-L-35-03.essay: Great blessings come through occupying a central and correct position.

XIANG-L-35-04.label: 35 晉 小象 3
XIANG-L-35-04.essay: The trust of the multitude allows an aspiration to move upward.

XIANG-L-35-05.label: 35 晉 小象 4
XIANG-L-35-05.essay: The grasping field mouse faces danger because its position is unsuitable.

XIANG-L-35-06.label: 35 晉 小象 5
XIANG-L-35-06.essay: Do not become consumed by gains or losses: proceeding with purpose can bring celebration.

XIANG-L-35-07.label: 35 晉 小象 6
XIANG-L-35-07.essay: Using strength only to discipline one's own city shows that the larger way has not yet shone fully.

XIANG-L-36-01.label: 36 明夷 大象
XIANG-L-36-01.original: 明入地中，明夷；君子以蒞眾，用晦而明。
XIANG-L-36-01.essay: Light enters Earth in Darkening of the Light. The exemplary person leads others with wisdom that does not always display itself.

XIANG-L-36-02.label: 36 明夷 小象 1
XIANG-L-36-02.essay: The traveler goes without food because loyalty to what is right outweighs personal comfort.

XIANG-L-36-03.label: 36 明夷 小象 2
XIANG-L-36-03.essay: The second line is fortunate because its responsiveness follows appropriate standards.

XIANG-L-36-04.label: 36 明夷 小象 3
XIANG-L-36-04.essay: The aim of the southern hunt is fulfilled when the principal source of harm is found.

XIANG-L-36-05.label: 36 明夷 小象 4
XIANG-L-36-05.essay: Entering the left side signifies gaining insight into the concealed intentions of the threatening power.

XIANG-L-36-06.label: 36 明夷 小象 5
XIANG-L-36-06.essay: Jizi's constancy shows that inner light must not be extinguished even when outward circumstances are dark.

XIANG-L-36-07.label: 36 明夷 小象 6
XIANG-L-36-07.original: 初登于天，照四國也。后入于地，失則也。
XIANG-L-36-07.essay: At first the light rose and illuminated the four regions; later it fell into darkness through loss of proper measure.

XIANG-L-37-01.label: 37 家人 大象
XIANG-L-37-01.original: 風自火出，家人；君子以言有物，而行有恆。
XIANG-L-37-01.essay: Wind issues from fire in The Family. The exemplary person speaks with substance and acts consistently.

XIANG-L-37-02.label: 37 家人 小象 1
XIANG-L-37-02.essay: Establishing household boundaries early prevents regret while intentions have not yet shifted.

XIANG-L-37-03.label: 37 家人 小象 2
XIANG-L-37-03.essay: The second line's good fortune comes from receptive and accommodating conduct.

XIANG-L-37-04.label: 37 家人 小象 3
XIANG-L-37-04.original: 家人嗃嗃，未失也；婦子嘻嘻，失家節也。
XIANG-L-37-04.essay: Firm household discipline is not necessarily mistaken; excessive joking without boundaries disrupts family order.

XIANG-L-37-05.label: 37 家人 小象 4
XIANG-L-37-05.essay: The prosperity of the household is fortunate because each person fulfills an appropriate position.

XIANG-L-37-06.label: 37 家人 小象 5
XIANG-L-37-06.essay: The ruler reaching the family shows reciprocal affection and mutual care.

XIANG-L-37-07.label: 37 家人 小象 6
XIANG-L-37-07.essay: Dignity brings good fortune when it begins with examining and correcting oneself.

XIANG-L-38-01.label: 38 睽 大象
XIANG-L-38-01.original: 上火下澤，睽；君子以同而異。
XIANG-L-38-01.essay: Fire rises while the lake lies below: Opposition. The exemplary person recognizes shared ground without erasing real differences.

XIANG-L-38-02.label: 38 睽 小象 1
XIANG-L-38-02.essay: Encountering a disagreeable person may prevent greater blame when handled with caution.

XIANG-L-38-03.label: 38 睽 小象 2
XIANG-L-38-03.essay: Meeting the master in a narrow lane does not mean the right course has been lost.

XIANG-L-38-04.label: 38 睽 小象 3
XIANG-L-38-04.original: 見輿曳，位不當也。无初有終，遇剛也。
XIANG-L-38-04.essay: A dragged carriage signals an unsuitable place. The difficult beginning can still end well when firmness is encountered.

XIANG-L-38-05.label: 38 睽 小象 4
XIANG-L-38-05.essay: Mutual trust overcomes estrangement and makes the purpose attainable.

XIANG-L-38-06.label: 38 睽 小象 5
XIANG-L-38-06.essay: Reunion with one's own kin allows forward movement to bring good fortune.

XIANG-L-38-07.label: 38 睽 小象 6
XIANG-L-38-07.essay: Rain dissolves the accumulated suspicions; what seemed hostile can become a fortunate meeting.

XIANG-L-39-01.label: 39 蹇 大象
XIANG-L-39-01.original: 山上有水，蹇；君子以反身修德。
XIANG-L-39-01.essay: Water stands above a mountain in Obstruction. The exemplary person turns inward to examine conduct and cultivate virtue.

XIANG-L-39-02.label: 39 蹇 小象 1
XIANG-L-39-02.essay: Forward movement encounters difficulty, while return earns respect. This is a time to wait.

XIANG-L-39-03.label: 39 蹇 小象 2
XIANG-L-39-03.essay: A minister struggles repeatedly for the ruler rather than personal advantage, and ultimately deserves no reproach.

XIANG-L-39-04.label: 39 蹇 小象 3
XIANG-L-39-04.essay: Returning from obstruction brings joy to those within one's circle.

XIANG-L-39-05.label: 39 蹇 小象 4
XIANG-L-39-05.essay: Returning to join others after difficulty is suitable because the position is solid.

XIANG-L-39-06.label: 39 蹇 小象 5
XIANG-L-39-06.essay: During great obstruction, companions arrive when one maintains a measured center.

XIANG-L-39-07.label: 39 蹇 小象 6
XIANG-L-39-07.original: 往蹇來碩，志在內也。利見大人，以從貴也。
XIANG-L-39-07.essay: Returning instead of forcing the road yields substance; seeking a worthy superior accords with the inward purpose.

XIANG-L-40-01.label: 40 解 大象
XIANG-L-40-01.original: 雷雨作，解；君子以赦過宥罪。
XIANG-L-40-01.essay: Thunder and rain break out in Release. The exemplary person pardons errors and treats offenses with measured leniency.

XIANG-L-40-02.label: 40 解 小象 1
XIANG-L-40-02.essay: At the meeting of firmness and gentleness, no blame arises when their relation is fitting.

XIANG-L-40-03.label: 40 解 小象 2
XIANG-L-40-03.essay: The second line's perseverance is fortunate because it has reached the middle way.

XIANG-L-40-04.label: 40 解 小象 3
XIANG-L-40-04.original: 負且乘，亦可丑也，自我致戎，又誰咎也。
XIANG-L-40-04.essay: Carrying a load while riding in privilege invites disgrace and attackers; one cannot blame others for risks produced by one's own behavior.

XIANG-L-40-05.label: 40 解 小象 4
XIANG-L-40-05.essay: Freeing the big toe indicates removal of a constraint, yet the present position is still not fully appropriate.

XIANG-L-40-06.label: 40 解 小象 5
XIANG-L-40-06.essay: When the exemplary person achieves release, petty and obstructive influences withdraw.

XIANG-L-40-07.label: 40 解 小象 6
XIANG-L-40-07.essay: The noble's shot at the hawk removes a disorderly source of trouble and restores proper order.

XIANG-L-41-01.label: 41 損 大象
XIANG-L-41-01.original: 山下有澤，損；君子以懲忿窒欲。
XIANG-L-41-01.essay: A lake lies below a mountain in Decrease. The exemplary person restrains anger and curbs excessive desires.

XIANG-L-41-02.label: 41 損 小象 1
XIANG-L-41-02.essay: Quickly assisting another after one's own duties are done brings the intention into accord with those above.

XIANG-L-41-03.label: 41 損 小象 2
XIANG-L-41-03.essay: The second line favors constancy because balance has become the core intention.

XIANG-L-41-04.label: 41 損 小象 3
XIANG-L-41-04.essay: When three travel together, suspicion may divide them; simpler companionship can allow trust to form.

XIANG-L-41-05.label: 41 損 小象 4
XIANG-L-41-05.essay: Removing an illness or defect is cause for joy, for decrease can be healing rather than deprivation.

XIANG-L-41-06.label: 41 損 小象 5
XIANG-L-41-06.essay: The fifth line's great fortune is described as help received from above.

XIANG-L-41-07.label: 41 損 小象 6
XIANG-L-41-07.essay: Helping others without unnecessary self-diminishment allows a significant aspiration to be fulfilled.

XIANG-L-42-01.label: 42 益 大象
XIANG-L-42-01.original: 風雷，益；君子以見善則遷，有過則改。
XIANG-L-42-01.essay: Wind and thunder combine in Increase. On seeing goodness, the exemplary person adopts it; on finding an error, corrects it.

XIANG-L-42-02.label: 42 益 小象 1
XIANG-L-42-02.essay: Great good fortune without blame reflects the need not to overload those in lower positions.

XIANG-L-42-03.label: 42 益 小象 2
XIANG-L-42-03.essay: Unexpected benefit arrives from outside, showing that increase is not always self-produced.

XIANG-L-42-04.label: 42 益 小象 3
XIANG-L-42-04.essay: Providing support during calamity belongs to one's established responsibilities.

XIANG-L-42-05.label: 42 益 小象 4
XIANG-L-42-05.essay: The duke accepts the report because it advances a beneficial purpose.

XIANG-L-42-06.label: 42 益 小象 5
XIANG-L-42-06.original: 有孚惠心，勿問之矣。惠我德，大得志也。
XIANG-L-42-06.essay: Sincere generosity need not be questioned; receiving goodwill in return greatly fulfills one's intention.

XIANG-L-42-07.label: 42 益 小象 6
XIANG-L-42-07.original: 莫益之，偏辭也。或擊之，自外來也。
XIANG-L-42-07.essay: No one helps and someone attacks because the words are partial; harm then arrives from outside.

XIANG-L-43-01.label: 43 夬 大象
XIANG-L-43-01.original: 澤上于天，夬；君子以施祿及下，居德則忌。
XIANG-L-43-01.essay: The lake rises into Heaven in Breakthrough. The exemplary person distributes benefits downward and avoids hoarding virtue as private property.

XIANG-L-43-02.label: 43 夬 小象 1
XIANG-L-43-02.essay: Advancing without being able to win produces blame; determination must be joined to capacity.

XIANG-L-43-03.label: 43 夬 小象 2
XIANG-L-43-03.essay: Even with soldiers appearing at night, a centered stance prevents panic.

XIANG-L-43-04.label: 43 夬 小象 3
XIANG-L-43-04.essay: The exemplary person's firm resolve ultimately avoids blame when it serves what is right.

XIANG-L-43-05.label: 43 夬 小象 4
XIANG-L-43-05.original: 其行次且，位不當也。聞言不信，聰不明也。
XIANG-L-43-05.essay: Hesitant walking reflects an unsuitable position; refusing advice shows a failure to hear clearly.

XIANG-L-43-06.label: 43 夬 小象 5
XIANG-L-43-06.essay: Walking the middle way avoids blame, although the central intention has not yet become fully bright.

XIANG-L-43-07.label: 43 夬 小象 6
XIANG-L-43-07.essay: A final inability to call for help brings misfortune, for an isolated extreme cannot endure.

XIANG-L-44-01.label: 44 姤 大象
XIANG-L-44-01.original: 天下有風，姤；后以施命誥四方。
XIANG-L-44-01.essay: Wind moves beneath Heaven in Coming to Meet. The ruler spreads commands and announcements to the four directions.

XIANG-L-44-02.label: 44 姤 小象 1
XIANG-L-44-02.essay: The metal brake restrains the emerging yielding force so that it cannot advance unchecked.

XIANG-L-44-03.label: 44 姤 小象 2
XIANG-L-44-03.essay: Having a fish in the wrapper is not meant to extend to the guest; possession carries limits of proper use.

XIANG-L-44-04.label: 44 姤 小象 3
XIANG-L-44-04.essay: Difficult walking persists, but the person's progress has not been drawn into a binding entanglement.

XIANG-L-44-05.label: 44 姤 小象 4
XIANG-L-44-05.essay: The misfortune of having no fish reflects estrangement from the people.

XIANG-L-44-06.label: 44 姤 小象 5
XIANG-L-44-06.original: 九五含章，中正也。有隕自天，志不舍命也。
XIANG-L-44-06.essay: The fifth line holds inner refinement with central correctness; the unexpected gift from Heaven accords with continued devotion to duty.

XIANG-L-44-07.label: 44 姤 小象 6
XIANG-L-44-07.essay: Meeting only at the horn is frustrating because the uppermost position has reached its limit.

XIANG-L-45-01.label: 45 萃 大象
XIANG-L-45-01.original: 澤上于地，萃；君子以除戎器，戒不虞。
XIANG-L-45-01.essay: The lake gathers above Earth in Gathering Together. The exemplary person repairs defensive equipment and prepares against unexpected danger.

XIANG-L-45-02.label: 45 萃 小象 1
XIANG-L-45-02.essay: Chaos precedes the gathering because the participants' intentions are confused.

XIANG-L-45-03.label: 45 萃 小象 2
XIANG-L-45-03.essay: Being drawn together brings good fortune because the inner center has not changed.

XIANG-L-45-04.label: 45 萃 小象 3
XIANG-L-45-04.essay: Proceeding without blame is possible through accommodating those above.

XIANG-L-45-05.label: 45 萃 小象 4
XIANG-L-45-05.essay: Even a greatly fortunate gathering can arise from an unsuitable position; success does not eliminate structural weakness.

XIANG-L-45-06.label: 45 萃 小象 5
XIANG-L-45-06.essay: Occupying the gathering's leading position is not enough when the guiding intention has yet to shine.

XIANG-L-45-07.label: 45 萃 小象 6
XIANG-L-45-07.essay: Tears and lament express insecurity in relation to those above, not merely private sadness.

XIANG-L-46-01.label: 46 升 大象
XIANG-L-46-01.original: 地中生木，升；君子以順德，積小以高大。
XIANG-L-46-01.essay: Wood grows within Earth in Pushing Upward. The exemplary person follows virtue patiently, accumulating small gains into something great.

XIANG-L-46-02.label: 46 升 小象 1
XIANG-L-46-02.essay: The rise is auspicious because one's aspiration agrees with those in higher positions.

XIANG-L-46-03.label: 46 升 小象 2
XIANG-L-46-03.essay: The second line's sincerity brings happiness and receives a favorable response.

XIANG-L-46-04.label: 46 升 小象 3
XIANG-L-46-04.essay: Ascending into an empty town leaves no obstacle to cause hesitation.

XIANG-L-46-05.label: 46 升 小象 4
XIANG-L-46-05.essay: The king's sacrifice at Mount Qi is favorable because it follows the proper ceremonial course.

XIANG-L-46-06.label: 46 升 小象 5
XIANG-L-46-06.essay: Rising step by step through constancy brings great fulfillment of aspiration.

XIANG-L-46-07.label: 46 升 小象 6
XIANG-L-46-07.essay: Blindly striving upward at the top does not bring lasting wealth; ascent without measure eventually declines.

XIANG-L-47-01.label: 47 困 大象
XIANG-L-47-01.original: 澤无水，困；君子以致命遂志。
XIANG-L-47-01.essay: A lake without water signifies Oppression. The exemplary person is ready to risk life rather than abandon a worthy aspiration.

XIANG-L-47-02.label: 47 困 小象 1
XIANG-L-47-02.essay: Entering the dark valley reflects a condition where light and understanding are absent.

XIANG-L-47-03.label: 47 困 小象 2
XIANG-L-47-03.essay: Although constrained by food and drink, the central position contains the prospect of a blessing.

XIANG-L-47-04.label: 47 困 小象 3
XIANG-L-47-04.original: 據于蒺藜，乘剛也。入于其宮，不見其妻，不祥也。
XIANG-L-47-04.essay: Thorns cause suffering because a yielding line presses upon the firm; returning home to find no wife signals further misfortune.

XIANG-L-47-05.label: 47 困 小象 4
XIANG-L-47-05.original: 來徐徐，志在下也。雖不當位，有與也。
XIANG-L-47-05.essay: The slow approach shows concern for those below. Despite an unsuitable position, help and companionship remain possible.

XIANG-L-47-06.label: 47 困 小象 5
XIANG-L-47-06.original: 劓刖，志未得也。乃徐有說，以中直也。利用祭祀，受福也。
XIANG-L-47-06.essay: Mutilation and confinement signal unrealized aims; relief comes gradually through central honesty, and sacrifice expresses hope of blessing.

XIANG-L-47-07.label: 47 困 小象 6
XIANG-L-47-07.original: 困于葛藟，未當也。動悔，有悔，吉行也。
XIANG-L-47-07.essay: Entangled in vines at an unsuitable position, one fears moving; recognizing the error and then acting can bring fortune.

XIANG-L-48-01.label: 48 井 大象
XIANG-L-48-01.original: 木上有水，井；君子以勞民勸相。
XIANG-L-48-01.essay: Water is drawn up by wood in The Well. The exemplary person works for the people's livelihood and encourages mutual aid.

XIANG-L-48-02.label: 48 井 小象 1
XIANG-L-48-02.original: 井泥不食，下也。舊井无禽，時舍也。
XIANG-L-48-02.essay: A muddy well is unusable at the bottom; an abandoned well attracts no creatures because its time of use has passed.

XIANG-L-48-03.label: 48 井 小象 2
XIANG-L-48-03.essay: A shallow well holding only little fish has no effective support or companion to make it useful.

XIANG-L-48-04.label: 48 井 小象 3
XIANG-L-48-04.original: 井渫不食，行惻也。求王明，受福也。
XIANG-L-48-04.essay: A cleaned well left unused causes sorrow; an enlightened ruler could draw upon it and extend its benefits.

XIANG-L-48-05.label: 48 井 小象 4
XIANG-L-48-05.essay: Rebuilding the well lining avoids blame because the source of nourishment has been repaired.

XIANG-L-48-06.label: 48 井 小象 5
XIANG-L-48-06.essay: Cold, clear spring water is fit to drink because the position is central and correct.

XIANG-L-48-07.label: 48 井 小象 6
XIANG-L-48-07.essay: Great good fortune at the top indicates a well whose useful work has been fully accomplished.

XIANG-L-49-01.label: 49 革 大象
XIANG-L-49-01.original: 澤中有火，革；君子以治歷明時。
XIANG-L-49-01.essay: Fire within the lake signifies Revolution. The exemplary person orders the calendar and clarifies the proper seasons.

XIANG-L-49-02.label: 49 革 小象 1
XIANG-L-49-02.original: 鞏用黃牛，不可以有為也。
XIANG-L-49-02.essay: Binding with yellow oxhide indicates that action must not yet be taken.

XIANG-L-49-03.label: 49 革 小象 2
XIANG-L-49-03.essay: Changing matters when the appointed day arrives brings a praiseworthy result.

XIANG-L-49-04.label: 49 革 小象 3
XIANG-L-49-04.essay: A call for reform repeated and carefully confirmed leaves no need for reckless further action.

XIANG-L-49-05.label: 49 革 小象 4
XIANG-L-49-05.essay: Changing the mandate succeeds because the purpose is trusted.

XIANG-L-49-06.label: 49 革 小象 5
XIANG-L-49-06.essay: The great person's transformation is like the bright stripes of a tiger, unmistakable in its outward pattern.

XIANG-L-49-07.label: 49 革 小象 6
XIANG-L-49-07.original: 君子豹變，其文蔚也。小人革面，順以從君也。
XIANG-L-49-07.essay: The exemplary person's change resembles the rich markings of a leopard; the ordinary person's surface change reflects compliance with the ruler.

XIANG-L-50-01.label: 50 鼎 大象
XIANG-L-50-01.original: 木上有火，鼎；君子以正位凝命。
XIANG-L-50-01.essay: Fire burns above wood in The Cauldron. The exemplary person sets positions correctly and stabilizes the public mandate.

XIANG-L-50-02.label: 50 鼎 小象 1
XIANG-L-50-02.original: 鼎顛趾，未悖也。利出否，以從貴也。
XIANG-L-50-02.essay: Turning the cauldron's feet upward to expel waste is not a violation when it serves a higher purpose.

XIANG-L-50-03.label: 50 鼎 小象 2
XIANG-L-50-03.original: 鼎有實，慎所之也。我仇有疾，終无尤也。
XIANG-L-50-03.essay: A filled cauldron requires careful decisions about where to go; opposition cannot ultimately cause blame when conduct is prudent.

XIANG-L-50-04.label: 50 鼎 小象 3
XIANG-L-50-04.essay: When the handles of the cauldron change, its purpose and proper working are lost.

XIANG-L-50-05.label: 50 鼎 小象 4
XIANG-L-50-05.essay: Overturning the ruler's food shows the gravity of failing an entrusted responsibility.

XIANG-L-50-06.label: 50 鼎 小象 5
XIANG-L-50-06.essay: The yellow handles suggest a central position that gives the cauldron substantial integrity.

XIANG-L-50-07.label: 50 鼎 小象 6
XIANG-L-50-07.essay: The jade carrying bar above expresses measured harmony between firmness and gentleness.

XIANG-L-51-01.label: 51 震 大象
XIANG-L-51-01.original: 洊雷，震；君子以恐懼修省。
XIANG-L-51-01.essay: Repeated thunder is Shock. The exemplary person responds with awe, examining conduct and correcting faults.

XIANG-L-51-02.label: 51 震 小象 1
XIANG-L-51-02.original: 震來虩虩，恐致福也。笑言啞啞，后有則也。
XIANG-L-51-02.essay: Initial fear can bring blessing; calm laughter afterwards comes from regaining proper standards.

XIANG-L-51-03.label: 51 震 小象 2
XIANG-L-51-03.essay: Danger follows the second line because yielding strength has mounted a firm one.

XIANG-L-51-04.label: 51 震 小象 3
XIANG-L-51-04.essay: Disorientation after a shock shows that the position is unsuitable.

XIANG-L-51-05.label: 51 震 小象 4
XIANG-L-51-05.essay: Thunder sinking into mud shows that its force has not yet become clear or effective.

XIANG-L-51-06.label: 51 震 小象 5
XIANG-L-51-06.original: 震往來厲，危行也。其事在中，大无喪也。
XIANG-L-51-06.essay: Danger accompanies both coming and going, but attending to the central matter prevents major loss.

XIANG-L-51-07.label: 51 震 小象 6
XIANG-L-51-07.original: 震索索，中未得也。雖凶无咎，畏鄰戒也。
XIANG-L-51-07.essay: Severe trembling means the center has not been secured; fear prompted by a neighbor's danger can prevent personal blame.

XIANG-L-52-01.label: 52 艮 大象
XIANG-L-52-01.original: 兼山，艮；君子以思不出其位。
XIANG-L-52-01.essay: Two mountains together signify Keeping Still. The exemplary person keeps thoughts within the responsibilities of the present position.

XIANG-L-52-02.label: 52 艮 小象 1
XIANG-L-52-02.essay: Stopping the toes before movement has not yet abandoned what is right.

XIANG-L-52-03.label: 52 艮 小象 2
XIANG-L-52-03.essay: Failure to rescue the follower arises because the person will not withdraw and listen.

XIANG-L-52-04.label: 52 艮 小象 3
XIANG-L-52-04.essay: Stopping at the waist creates internal tension; danger burns painfully in the heart.

XIANG-L-52-05.label: 52 艮 小象 4
XIANG-L-52-05.essay: Stillness of the whole body restrains one's own actions and avoids misplaced intervention.

XIANG-L-52-06.label: 52 艮 小象 5
XIANG-L-52-06.essay: Controlling the jaws brings orderly speech because balance and correctness guide expression.

XIANG-L-52-07.label: 52 艮 小象 6
XIANG-L-52-07.essay: Generous stillness at the top is fortunate because restraint is maintained to a substantial conclusion.

XIANG-L-53-01.label: 53 漸 大象
XIANG-L-53-01.original: 山上有木，漸；君子以居賢德，善俗。
XIANG-L-53-01.essay: A tree grows upon a mountain in Gradual Development. The exemplary person cultivates worthy character and improves communal customs.

XIANG-L-53-02.label: 53 漸 小象 1
XIANG-L-53-02.essay: The young person's danger is not blameworthy when judged in its proper circumstances.

XIANG-L-53-03.label: 53 漸 小象 2
XIANG-L-53-03.essay: Eating and drinking cheerfully is not merely enjoying unearned food; support corresponds to a fitting place.

XIANG-L-53-04.label: 53 漸 小象 3
XIANG-L-53-04.original: 夫征不復，離群丑也。婦孕不育，失其道也。利用禦寇，順相保也。
XIANG-L-53-04.essay: The absent husband has left his group; the failed pregnancy reflects a lost course. Defense succeeds when companions protect one another.

XIANG-L-53-05.label: 53 漸 小象 4
XIANG-L-53-05.essay: A goose finding a stable branch avoids blame through compliant and gentle adaptation.

XIANG-L-53-06.label: 53 漸 小象 5
XIANG-L-53-06.essay: An obstacle cannot defeat the gradual approach in the end, and the long-awaited desire is fulfilled.

XIANG-L-53-07.label: 53 漸 小象 6
XIANG-L-53-07.original: 其羽可用為儀，吉；不可亂也。
XIANG-L-53-07.essay: The goose's feathers become ceremonial ornaments; their orderly use must not be disturbed.

XIANG-L-54-01.label: 54 歸妹 大象
XIANG-L-54-01.original: 澤上有雷，歸妹；君子以永終知敝。
XIANG-L-54-01.essay: Thunder sounds above the lake in The Marrying Maiden. The exemplary person considers long-term consequences and the ways relationships can deteriorate.

XIANG-L-54-02.label: 54 歸妹 小象 1
XIANG-L-54-02.original: 歸妹以娣，以恆也。跛能履吉，相承也。
XIANG-L-54-02.essay: Marriage as a younger attendant reflects established custom; even limited ability can serve when roles support each other.

XIANG-L-54-03.label: 54 歸妹 小象 2
XIANG-L-54-03.essay: Constancy in solitude is favorable because the ordinary principles have not changed.

XIANG-L-54-04.label: 54 歸妹 小象 3
XIANG-L-54-04.essay: The maiden's unsuitable role means the attempted marriage is not properly timed or placed.

XIANG-L-54-05.label: 54 歸妹 小象 4
XIANG-L-54-05.essay: A postponed wedding may express a deliberate decision to wait until action is appropriate.

XIANG-L-54-06.label: 54 歸妹 小象 5
XIANG-L-54-06.original: 帝乙歸妹，不如其娣之袂良也。其位在中，以貴行也。
XIANG-L-54-06.essay: King Di Yi's marriage arrangement values central rank over splendid sleeves; the historical image distinguishes status from outward finery.

XIANG-L-54-07.label: 54 歸妹 小象 6
XIANG-L-54-07.essay: The final line carries an empty basket, showing that the ceremony lacks the substance it requires.

XIANG-L-55-01.label: 55 豐 大象
XIANG-L-55-01.original: 雷電皆至，豐；君子以折獄致刑。
XIANG-L-55-01.essay: Thunder and lightning arrive together in Abundance. The exemplary person settles legal cases clearly and imposes penalties with discernment.

XIANG-L-55-02.label: 55 豐 小象 1
XIANG-L-55-02.essay: Ten days together cause no blame, but exceeding that time brings trouble; abundance also has limits.

XIANG-L-55-03.label: 55 豐 小象 2
XIANG-L-55-03.essay: Sincerity brightens the situation and allows genuine aims to become known.

XIANG-L-55-04.label: 55 豐 小象 3
XIANG-L-55-04.original: 豐其沛，不可大事也。折其右肱，終不可用也。
XIANG-L-55-04.essay: Thick screens obscure judgment, and a broken right arm makes great endeavors impossible.

XIANG-L-55-05.label: 55 豐 小象 4
XIANG-L-55-05.original: 豐其蔀，位不當也。日中見斗，幽不明也。遇其夷主，吉；行也。
XIANG-L-55-05.essay: The screen hides daylight because the position is unsuitable; meeting an appropriate equal opens a way forward.

XIANG-L-55-06.label: 55 豐 小象 5
XIANG-L-55-06.essay: The fifth line's fortunate result brings celebration and public honor.

XIANG-L-55-07.label: 55 豐 小象 6
XIANG-L-55-07.original: 豐其屋，天際翔也。窺其戶，闃其无人，自藏也。
XIANG-L-55-07.essay: A towering house that hides its empty interior reflects self-isolation; its owner has concealed himself from human contact.

XIANG-L-56-01.label: 56 旅 大象
XIANG-L-56-01.original: 山上有火，旅；君子以明慎用刑，而不留獄。
XIANG-L-56-01.essay: Fire burns on a mountain in The Wanderer. The exemplary person applies penalties carefully and does not let lawsuits or imprisonment linger.

XIANG-L-56-02.label: 56 旅 小象 1
XIANG-L-56-02.essay: Petty preoccupation during travel brings disaster when aspirations have reached a dead end.

XIANG-L-56-03.label: 56 旅 小象 2
XIANG-L-56-03.essay: A loyal young attendant ultimately brings no reproach to the wanderer.

XIANG-L-56-04.label: 56 旅 小象 3
XIANG-L-56-04.original: 旅焚其次，亦以傷矣。以旅與下，其義喪也。
XIANG-L-56-04.essay: A burned lodging is already a loss; harsh treatment of dependents while away makes the situation worse.

XIANG-L-56-05.label: 56 旅 小象 4
XIANG-L-56-05.original: 旅于處，未得位也。得其資斧，心未快也。
XIANG-L-56-05.essay: Lodging and tools are obtained, but the traveler still lacks a secure position and remains unhappy.

XIANG-L-56-06.label: 56 旅 小象 5
XIANG-L-56-06.essay: The wanderer's eventual reputation and appointment reach those in higher authority.

XIANG-L-56-07.label: 56 旅 小象 6
XIANG-L-56-07.original: 以旅在上，其義焚也。喪牛于易，終莫之聞也。
XIANG-L-56-07.essay: A wanderer at the summit has no stable home; losing the ox without awareness signals a severe failure of judgment.

XIANG-L-57-01.label: 57 巽 大象
XIANG-L-57-01.original: 隨風，巽；君子以申命行事。
XIANG-L-57-01.essay: Following winds signify Gentle Penetration. The exemplary person repeats important commands and carries them into action.

XIANG-L-57-02.label: 57 巽 小象 1
XIANG-L-57-02.original: 進退，志疑也。利武人之貞，志治也。
XIANG-L-57-02.essay: Indecision reveals a doubtful purpose; disciplined firmness restores direction.

XIANG-L-57-03.label: 57 巽 小象 2
XIANG-L-57-03.essay: The auspicious outcome of many ritual attendants rests on finding the middle way.

XIANG-L-57-04.label: 57 巽 小象 3
XIANG-L-57-04.essay: Repeatedly yielding without conviction is regrettable because aspiration has become exhausted.

XIANG-L-57-05.label: 57 巽 小象 4
XIANG-L-57-05.essay: Three kinds of game obtained in the hunt show that determined action has achieved results.

XIANG-L-57-06.label: 57 巽 小象 5
XIANG-L-57-06.essay: The fifth line's good fortune follows from occupying the correct central position.

XIANG-L-57-07.label: 57 巽 小象 6
XIANG-L-57-07.original: 巽在牀下，上窮也。喪其資斧，正乎凶也。
XIANG-L-57-07.essay: Crouching under the bed at the extreme leaves one helpless; losing resources and an axe confirms the danger of excessive submission.

XIANG-L-58-01.label: 58 兌 大象
XIANG-L-58-01.original: 麗澤，兌；君子以朋友講習。
XIANG-L-58-01.essay: Two lakes joined together signify Joy. The exemplary person studies and discusses matters with friends so that learning deepens.

XIANG-L-58-02.label: 58 兌 小象 1
XIANG-L-58-02.essay: Harmonious joy is fortunate because action is free from suspicion.

XIANG-L-58-03.label: 58 兌 小象 2
XIANG-L-58-03.essay: Joy founded on trust is fortunate because the intention is sincere.

XIANG-L-58-04.label: 58 兌 小象 3
XIANG-L-58-04.essay: Joy pursued by ingratiation is unfortunate because the person occupies an unsuitable position.

XIANG-L-58-05.label: 58 兌 小象 4
XIANG-L-58-05.essay: The fourth line's happiness carries a promise of celebration after a difficult choice.

XIANG-L-58-06.label: 58 兌 小象 5
XIANG-L-58-06.essay: Trust placed in a destructive influence brings danger even to one in a correct position.

XIANG-L-58-07.label: 58 兌 小象 6
XIANG-L-58-07.essay: At the top, drawing others into pleasure has not yet displayed genuine moral brightness.

XIANG-L-59-01.label: 59 渙 大象
XIANG-L-59-01.original: 風行水上，渙；先王以享于帝立廟。
XIANG-L-59-01.essay: Wind moves across water in Dispersion. Earlier kings offered sacrifice to Heaven and established ancestral temples to renew a shared center.

XIANG-L-59-02.label: 59 渙 小象 1
XIANG-L-59-02.essay: The first line's rescue is fortunate because it responds promptly and cooperatively.

XIANG-L-59-03.label: 59 渙 小象 2
XIANG-L-59-03.essay: Running to the support of the table brings fulfillment of a deeply held wish.

XIANG-L-59-04.label: 59 渙 小象 3
XIANG-L-59-04.essay: Dispersing personal attachments directs one's purpose beyond private self-interest.

XIANG-L-59-05.label: 59 渙 小象 4
XIANG-L-59-05.essay: Dispersing a narrow faction brings great good fortune because a wider common purpose becomes possible.

XIANG-L-59-06.label: 59 渙 小象 5
XIANG-L-59-06.essay: The ruler's residence is without blame when authority occupies its proper place.

XIANG-L-59-07.label: 59 渙 小象 6
XIANG-L-59-07.essay: Dispersing bloodshed and fleeing danger keeps harm at a distance.

XIANG-L-60-01.label: 60 節 大象
XIANG-L-60-01.original: 澤上有水，節；君子以制數度，議德行。
XIANG-L-60-01.essay: Water rests above a lake in Limitation. The exemplary person sets measures and standards and deliberates about virtuous conduct.

XIANG-L-60-02.label: 60 節 小象 1
XIANG-L-60-02.essay: Remaining inside the courtyard avoids blame because one understands when passage is open and when it is blocked.

XIANG-L-60-03.label: 60 節 小象 2
XIANG-L-60-03.essay: Refusing to leave even the gate becomes unfortunate when the crucial opportunity has been missed.

XIANG-L-60-04.label: 60 節 小象 3
XIANG-L-60-04.essay: The person who refuses all restraint has cause to lament; that failing cannot simply be blamed on others.

XIANG-L-60-05.label: 60 節 小象 4
XIANG-L-60-05.essay: Peaceful limitation prospers because it follows a worthy higher principle.

XIANG-L-60-06.label: 60 節 小象 5
XIANG-L-60-06.essay: Sweet and fitting restraint is fortunate because it occupies a balanced position.

XIANG-L-60-07.label: 60 節 小象 6
XIANG-L-60-07.essay: Harsh restriction pursued without change reaches a dead end; bitter limits cannot endure.

XIANG-L-61-01.label: 61 中孚 大象
XIANG-L-61-01.original: 澤上有風，中孚；君子以議獄緩死。
XIANG-L-61-01.essay: Wind moves over the lake in Inner Truth. The exemplary person deliberates carefully in legal matters and delays irreversible death sentences.

XIANG-L-61-02.label: 61 中孚 小象 1
XIANG-L-61-02.essay: Prudent preparation is fortunate because the initial intention has not been changed.

XIANG-L-61-03.label: 61 中孚 小象 2
XIANG-L-61-03.essay: A young crane echoes its parent because the response arises sincerely from within.

XIANG-L-61-04.label: 61 中孚 小象 3
XIANG-L-61-04.essay: Indecisive drumming or silence reflects an unsuitable position and wavering confidence.

XIANG-L-61-05.label: 61 中孚 小象 4
XIANG-L-61-05.essay: Losing the paired horses symbolizes leaving one's own circle to turn toward a higher commitment.

XIANG-L-61-06.label: 61 中孚 小象 5
XIANG-L-61-06.essay: Trust binds people together without blame because the position is correct.

XIANG-L-61-07.label: 61 中孚 小象 6
XIANG-L-61-07.essay: The rooster's call cannot truly rise to Heaven; boastful sound without matching substance cannot last.

XIANG-L-62-01.label: 62 小過 大象
XIANG-L-62-01.original: 山上有雷，小過；君子以行過乎恭，喪過乎哀，用過乎儉。
XIANG-L-62-01.essay: Thunder rises above a mountain in Small Exceeding. The exemplary person leans toward added respect, sincere mourning, and economical daily use.

XIANG-L-62-02.label: 62 小過 小象 1
XIANG-L-62-02.essay: A bird flying too high meets disaster that can no longer readily be prevented.

XIANG-L-62-03.label: 62 小過 小象 2
XIANG-L-62-03.essay: Stopping short of the ruler and meeting the minister observes a boundary that subjects should not overstep.

XIANG-L-62-04.label: 62 小過 小象 3
XIANG-L-62-04.essay: Careless following leaves a person exposed to violence; the danger can be severe.

XIANG-L-62-05.label: 62 小過 小象 4
XIANG-L-62-05.original: 弗過遇之，位不當也。往厲必戒，終不可長也。
XIANG-L-62-05.essay: A suitable meeting avoids blame, but going forward is perilous; continued vigilance is needed because the condition cannot last.

XIANG-L-62-06.label: 62 小過 小象 5
XIANG-L-62-06.essay: Dense clouds fail to produce rain because the force has risen too high.

XIANG-L-62-07.label: 62 小過 小象 6
XIANG-L-62-07.essay: Passing beyond the proper meeting point is excessive ascent, inviting the bird's misfortune.

XIANG-L-63-01.label: 63 既濟 大象
XIANG-L-63-01.original: 水在火上，既濟；君子以思患而豫防之。
XIANG-L-63-01.essay: Water stands above fire in After Completion. The exemplary person anticipates future trouble and prepares before it arrives.

XIANG-L-63-02.label: 63 既濟 小象 1
XIANG-L-63-02.essay: Holding back the wheels is right and causes no blame; early caution protects what is already achieved.

XIANG-L-63-03.label: 63 既濟 小象 2
XIANG-L-63-03.essay: What is lost returns after seven days because patience follows a balanced course.

XIANG-L-63-04.label: 63 既濟 小象 3
XIANG-L-63-04.essay: Three years of campaigning bring victory, but the long struggle has exhausted those involved.

XIANG-L-63-05.label: 63 既濟 小象 4
XIANG-L-63-05.essay: Remaining alert throughout the day reflects awareness of possible dangers beneath apparent success.

XIANG-L-63-06.label: 63 既濟 小象 5
XIANG-L-63-06.original: 東鄰殺牛，不如西鄰之時也；實受其福，吉大來也。
XIANG-L-63-06.essay: The eastern neighbor's lavish ox sacrifice is less timely than the western neighbor's modest rite; true blessing follows appropriate timing.

XIANG-L-63-07.label: 63 既濟 小象 6
XIANG-L-63-07.essay: When the head is immersed, danger is immediate; that degree of overreach cannot continue.

XIANG-L-64-01.label: 64 未濟 大象
XIANG-L-64-01.original: 火在水上，未濟；君子以慎辨物居方。
XIANG-L-64-01.essay: Fire rests above water in Before Completion. The exemplary person carefully distinguishes things and assigns each its appropriate place.

XIANG-L-64-02.label: 64 未濟 小象 1
XIANG-L-64-02.essay: Wetting the tail shows failure to recognize the limit of what can safely be attempted.

XIANG-L-64-03.label: 64 未濟 小象 2
XIANG-L-64-03.essay: The second line is fortunate because moderation guides action along the correct course.

XIANG-L-64-04.label: 64 未濟 小象 3
XIANG-L-64-04.essay: Advancing before completion is dangerous because the present position does not fit the task.

XIANG-L-64-05.label: 64 未濟 小象 4
XIANG-L-64-05.essay: Steadfastness ends regret, allowing the underlying aspiration to be carried out.

XIANG-L-64-06.label: 64 未濟 小象 5
XIANG-L-64-06.essay: The exemplary person's light spreads brightness and brings good fortune to others.

XIANG-L-64-07.label: 64 未濟 小象 6
XIANG-L-64-07.essay: Drinking until the head is soaked reveals a failure to recognize moderation and proper limits.

WENYAN-01-01.label: 01 乾 文言 1
WENYAN-01-01.original: 元者，善之長也。亨者，嘉之會也。利者，義之和也。貞者，事之幹也。君子體仁足以長人，嘉會足以合禮，利物足以和義，貞固足以幹事。君子行此四德者，故曰：「乾，元、亨、利、貞。」
WENYAN-01-01.essay: Yuan is the beginning and leading force of goodness; heng is the gathering of favorable conditions; li is the harmony between benefit and what is right; and zhen is the firm foundation on which affairs can be completed. A cultivated person embodies compassion in leading others, brings people together in a manner consistent with proper conduct, benefits things without violating justice, and remains steadfast when carrying out responsibilities. These are not four promises of effortless success. They describe four qualities that make constructive action possible. The Qian hexagram is therefore characterized by yuan, heng, li, and zhen.

WENYAN-01-02.label: 01 乾 文言 2
WENYAN-01-02.original: 初九曰：「潛龍，勿用。」何謂也？子曰：「龍德而隱者也。不易乎世，不成乎名，遯世无悶，不見是而无悶，樂則行之，憂則違之，確乎其不可拔，潛龍也。」
WENYAN-01-02.essay: The hidden dragon represents someone with exceptional character who has not yet stepped into public view. Such a person does not change convictions simply to follow fashion or rush to secure recognition. Living apart from public affairs need not cause resentment, and being overlooked need not lead to bitterness. One acts when doing so accords with one's principles and refrains when the circumstances are troubling. The decisive quality is an inner resolve that cannot easily be uprooted. The image of the concealed dragon thus presents restraint as a positive expression of strength, not as evidence of weakness.

WENYAN-01-03.label: 01 乾 文言 3
WENYAN-01-03.original: 九二曰：「見龍在田，利見大人。」何謂也？子曰：「龍德而正中者也。庸言之信，庸行之謹；閑邪存其誠，善世而不伐，德博而化。易曰：『見龍在田，利見大人。』君德也。」
WENYAN-01-03.essay: The dragon appearing in the field describes a person of sound character whose influence is beginning to become visible. Trustworthiness should be evident in everyday speech, care in ordinary actions, and sincerity in resisting dishonest impulses. A person can contribute to the welfare of society without boasting of those contributions. When conduct is consistently good, its influence can spread beyond the individual. The commentary calls this the virtue appropriate to a ruler: moral authority begins with how someone behaves in unremarkable situations, well before power and public reputation become prominent.

WENYAN-01-04.label: 01 乾 文言 4
WENYAN-01-04.original: 九三曰：「君子終日乾乾，夕惕若，厲，无咎。」何謂也？子曰：「君子進德脩業。忠信，所以進德也；脩辭立其誠，所以居業也。知至至之，可與言幾也。知終終之，可與存義也。是故居上位而不驕，在下位而不憂，故乾乾因其時而惕，雖危无咎矣。」
WENYAN-01-04.essay: The third line portrays a conscientious person working diligently throughout the day and remaining watchful at night. The explanation links this vigilance to the cultivation of character and the responsible pursuit of work. Loyalty and trust develop virtue, while thoughtful language and sincerity help sustain meaningful undertakings. One should recognize the early signs of an opportunity and know when to advance, but also recognize when an undertaking has reached its proper end. Neither holding a higher position nor occupying a lower one should produce arrogance or despair. Attentiveness to changing circumstances makes it possible to navigate danger without incurring blame.

WENYAN-01-05.label: 01 乾 文言 5
WENYAN-01-05.original: 九四曰：「或躍在淵，无咎。」何謂也？子曰：「上下无常，非為邪也。進退无恒，非離羣也。君子進德脩業，欲及時也。故无咎。」
WENYAN-01-05.essay: The dragon that may leap but still remains near the depths illustrates a period of uncertain transition. Moving up or down does not by itself indicate dishonesty, and changing between advance and withdrawal does not necessarily mean abandoning one's companions. A thoughtful person continues to develop abilities and character while waiting for a fitting opportunity. The essential point is to distinguish flexibility from opportunism. An action may be right at one moment and premature at another. Because the person responds to the time rather than forcing a fixed course, the text says that blame can be avoided.

WENYAN-01-06.label: 01 乾 文言 6
WENYAN-01-06.original: 九五曰：「飛龍在天，利見大人。」何謂也？子曰：「同聲相應，同氣相求；水流濕，火就燥，雲從龍，風從虎；聖人作而萬物覩；本乎天者親上，本乎地者親下，則各從其類也。」
WENYAN-01-06.essay: When the dragon flies in the sky, its influence is fully visible. The commentary explains this by observing that similar sounds answer one another and similar energies seek each other out. Water flows toward damp ground, fire takes readily to dry material, clouds accompany the dragon, and wind accompanies the tiger. In the same way, when a sage emerges, others perceive and respond to that person's influence. Beings associated with heaven tend upward, while those associated with earth tend downward. The image emphasizes resonance and natural affinity rather than the idea that public authority can be established through force alone.

WENYAN-01-07.label: 01 乾 文言 7
WENYAN-01-07.original: 上九曰：「亢龍，有悔。」何謂也？子曰：「貴而无位，高而无民，賢人在下位而无輔，是以動而有悔也。」
WENYAN-01-07.essay: The dragon that climbs too high reaches a precarious condition. Someone may appear distinguished yet lack a secure and legitimate position, stand above others without their support, or be surrounded by capable people who are unable or unwilling to help. Height and prestige are therefore not sufficient measures of sound leadership. Once a person becomes isolated from both ordinary people and trustworthy advisers, taking further action can bring regret. The warning concerns overextension: a position that looks impressive may already have lost the relationships and foundations needed to sustain it.

WENYAN-01-08.label: 01 乾 文言 8
WENYAN-01-08.essay: The expression 'Hidden dragon; do not act' indicates a condition of being below or out of public sight. This does not condemn the person's abilities. It says that those abilities have not yet reached the stage at which they can be exercised openly. The location of the first line helps explain the restraint called for in the original judgment. Recognizing a low or preliminary position is part of recognizing the correct time for action. The emphasis is on patient preparation, not permanent withdrawal.

WENYAN-01-09.label: 01 乾 文言 9
WENYAN-01-09.essay: 'The dragon appears in the field' marks a time when valuable character can begin to be recognized. The phrase 'the time allows it to remain' suggests that the emerging individual has found a place where talents may be displayed without rushing beyond the circumstances. Unlike the hidden dragon, this stage permits contact with others and the beginnings of public influence. Yet the position is still one of development rather than complete authority. The lesson lies in accepting the opportunities available at this particular stage.

WENYAN-01-10.label: 01 乾 文言 10
WENYAN-01-10.essay: 'Diligent throughout the day' points to someone actively engaged in responsibilities. The language is not merely a compliment about being busy. It places continued effort within a phase when decisions and conduct can have consequences. Work requires attention, persistence, and an awareness that one's position is changing. The accompanying warning about vigilance is therefore meaningful: activity should be sustained by reflection rather than performed mechanically. The line describes an active stage of cultivation and practical engagement.

WENYAN-01-11.label: 01 乾 文言 11
WENYAN-01-11.essay: 'Perhaps leaping, yet remaining in the depths' describes a person testing whether the time is right to rise. The commentary's brief explanation, 'testing oneself,' emphasizes uncertainty rather than failure. Abilities may be ready, but circumstances still need to be assessed. A trial movement may reveal whether advancement is appropriate, and hesitation may prevent a premature commitment. The image captures the point between private preparation and full public action, when judgment matters as much as courage.

WENYAN-01-12.label: 01 乾 文言 12
WENYAN-01-12.essay: 'The dragon flies in the sky' signifies effective governance from a higher position. The commentary shifts attention from the mere image of height to its public consequences: someone who has reached the appropriate level can now exercise responsibility. Visibility must be matched by the capacity to bring order and benefit to others. The image is therefore not simply about promotion or personal success. It concerns the stage at which developed virtue and ability are placed where they can shape collective affairs.

WENYAN-01-13.label: 01 乾 文言 13
WENYAN-01-13.essay: 'The overreaching dragon has regret' warns of the distress that follows when development passes its sustainable limit. The phrase 'the calamity of exhaustion' describes a situation in which further progress is no longer possible on the same terms. A person who has reached the extreme may mistake height for permanence and overlook the signs of decline. The statement offers a compact explanation of the warning in the top line: without an awareness of limits, apparent achievement can turn into misfortune.

WENYAN-01-14.label: 01 乾 文言 14
WENYAN-01-14.essay: 'Qian's use of the nines' is explained as a condition in which the world is well ordered. Unlike the image of a solitary ruler standing above the rest, this statement points to the coordinated operation of strong forces. Its brevity should not obscure the distinction: the mature use of strength is not endless competition to become first. It is the proper arrangement of capacities so that order becomes possible. The passage interprets the special 'use of nine' statement in terms of governance rather than individual display.

WENYAN-01-15.label: 01 乾 文言 15
WENYAN-01-15.essay: 'Hidden dragon; do not act' is here explained through the language of energy: the yang force remains concealed. The commentary describes the natural condition of an emerging power before it has become manifest. Something can exist and be developing even when it cannot yet be seen. The first stage of Qian is thus a time for conserving and forming strength. Bringing it prematurely into the open would ignore the relationship between development and timing. Concealment is part of the process, not necessarily an obstacle to it.

WENYAN-01-16.label: 01 乾 文言 16
WENYAN-01-16.essay: 'The dragon appears in the field' is associated here with the world becoming illuminated and civilized. The commentary broadens the earlier account of personal virtue into a social image: when constructive abilities come into view, they can begin to influence the surrounding world. The dragon's appearance does not mean the process is complete. Rather, it marks the emergence of a force whose effects may now be recognized. The emphasis falls on the public visibility of positive character and the gradual spread of its influence.

WENYAN-01-17.label: 01 乾 文言 17
WENYAN-01-17.essay: 'Diligent throughout the day' is interpreted as keeping pace with the time. Constant effort has value because it responds to developing circumstances rather than resisting change. A cultivated person must neither rest upon earlier achievements nor move blindly without observing what has altered. This stage calls for steady work, continual learning, and vigilance. To move with the time means bringing one's conduct into line with what the moment requires. The commentary thus connects diligence with adaptability.

WENYAN-01-18.label: 01 乾 文言 18
WENYAN-01-18.essay: 'Perhaps leaping, yet remaining in the depths' signifies a turning point in the Way of Qian. The image portrays neither settled withdrawal nor secure ascendance. It is the moment when an established pattern begins to change and a different level of action becomes possible. Because the transformation has not yet been completed, certainty would be misplaced. The commentary encourages awareness of the transition itself: when the underlying conditions shift, the way strength is expressed must also change.

WENYAN-01-19.label: 01 乾 文言 19
WENYAN-01-19.essay: 'The dragon flies in the sky' means that a person has reached a position from which heavenly virtue can be expressed. The focus is not on height alone. The appropriate position enables a cultivated individual to put the qualities of Qian into practice in a visible and consequential manner. Strength, sound judgment, and responsibility should now be apparent in conduct. This stage differs from the hidden or testing stages because capacity and opportunity have come together.

WENYAN-01-20.label: 01 乾 文言 20
WENYAN-01-20.essay: 'The overreaching dragon has regret' is linked to the time itself reaching an extreme. Even a successful development has a limit. When the circumstances that sustained an ascent have been exhausted, continuing to rise in the same manner becomes hazardous. The commentary treats excess as a temporal condition as well as a personal failing. Wise action requires noticing when a period is ending, rather than believing that its earlier momentum will continue indefinitely.

WENYAN-01-21.label: 01 乾 文言 21
WENYAN-01-21.essay: 'Qian's use of the nines' allows the pattern of heaven to be seen. The phrase points beyond any single dragon or individual achievement to the principles governing the whole process. Strength is expressed through change, timing, and the proper relation among different stages. Observing all the lines together makes that pattern clearer. The special statement therefore invites the reader to understand Qian as an ordered movement of forces rather than a command to dominate others.

WENYAN-01-22.label: 01 乾 文言 22
WENYAN-01-22.original: 乾元者，始而亨者也。利貞者，性情也。乾始能以美利利天下，不言所利，大矣哉！大哉乾元，剛健中正，純粹精也。六爻發揮，旁通情也。時乘六龍，以御天也。雲行雨施，天下平也。
WENYAN-01-22.essay: The originating force of Qian allows things to begin and develop; benefit and steadfastness express the character and proper direction of that development. Qian bestows benefits widely without restricting them to a favored recipient. Its greatness rests on vigor, balance, rectitude, and purity. The six lines reveal different situations through which this force may unfold. The six dragons, moving with their proper times, symbolize the ordering of heavenly processes. Clouds travel, rain falls, and the world is brought into harmony. The passage presents creative strength as generative and widely beneficial, not as mere forcefulness.

WENYAN-01-23.label: 01 乾 文言 23
WENYAN-01-23.original: 君子以成德為行，日可見之行也。潛之為言也，隱而未見，行而未成，是以君子弗用也。
WENYAN-01-23.essay: A cultivated person's actions should make acquired virtue visible in daily life. Yet the image of hiding has a specific meaning: character may have developed privately without having reached a form ready for public expression. The work is not complete simply because the intention is good. In the first stage, withdrawal helps protect an unfinished undertaking. The text therefore distinguishes possessing potential from having the conditions and demonstrated practice needed to use it. Restraint can be faithful to the goal of mature action.

WENYAN-01-24.label: 01 乾 文言 24
WENYAN-01-24.original: 君子學以聚之，問以辯之，寬以居之，仁以行之，易曰：「見龍在田，利見大人。」君德也。
WENYAN-01-24.essay: A cultivated person gathers understanding through study, clarifies it by asking questions, receives others with generosity, and puts it into action through benevolence. These four practices connect learning with ethical conduct. Knowledge alone is insufficient if it is not tested by inquiry and translated into how others are treated. The passage uses these qualities to explain the dragon appearing in the field: the virtues appropriate to leadership are already taking shape through education, openness, and practical care. Public influence should grow from that foundation.

WENYAN-01-25.label: 01 乾 文言 25
WENYAN-01-25.original: 九三，重剛而不中，上不在天，下不在田；故乾乾因其時而惕，雖危，无咎矣。
WENYAN-01-25.essay: The third line contains strong yang energy but does not occupy a central position. It stands above the field without yet reaching the domain of heaven. That unstable middle condition explains why the person must work energetically and remain alert. Neither status nor circumstances offer complete security. Vigilance does not mean panic; it means recognizing the particular risks of an intermediate stage. Even when danger exists, disciplined conduct can prevent blame. The passage reads the line's demanding language through its place in the six-line structure.

WENYAN-01-26.label: 01 乾 文言 26
WENYAN-01-26.original: 九四，重剛而不中，上不在天，下不在田，中不在人，故或之。或之者，疑之也，故无咎。
WENYAN-01-26.essay: The fourth line is also strongly yang but not central. It is no longer situated in the field below, has not yet arrived at heaven above, and does not neatly occupy the ordinary human position between them. That uncertainty is why the line says 'perhaps.' The word signals an unresolved choice about advancing or remaining where one is. A cautious trial or pause is appropriate while the situation remains ambiguous. The commentary treats doubt as a feature of transition, and careful judgment as the way to avoid blame.

WENYAN-01-27.label: 01 乾 文言 27
WENYAN-01-27.original: 夫大人者，與天地合其德，與日月合其明，與四時合其序，與鬼神合其吉凶；先天而天弗違，後天而奉天時，天且弗違，而況於人乎？況於鬼神乎？
WENYAN-01-27.essay: A great person brings conduct into accord with the virtue of heaven and earth, with the brightness of sun and moon, and with the succession of the seasons. Even the traditional language of spirits and good or bad fortune points to this comprehensive harmony. Acting ahead of an event does not violate the heavenly pattern, while acting afterward still observes the proper time. The passage describes an ideal of wisdom so thoroughly attuned to change that action is neither premature nor belated. Its claims belong to the philosophical and cosmological language of the text, rather than to a testable promise of prediction.

WENYAN-01-28.label: 01 乾 文言 28
WENYAN-01-28.original: 亢之為言也，知進而不知退，知存而不知亡，知得而不知喪；其唯聖人乎？知進退存亡而不失其正者，其唯聖人乎！
WENYAN-01-28.essay: To be excessively high is to know only how to advance, not how to withdraw; to notice continued existence but forget the possibility of loss; and to value gain without preparing for deprivation. Such one-sided thinking creates the danger expressed by the overreaching dragon. The passage closes by praising the rare person who understands advance and retreat, survival and decline, gain and loss, while still preserving what is right. True wisdom is not unlimited expansion. It is the ability to recognize opposing possibilities and act without abandoning sound principles.

WENYAN-02-01.label: 02 坤 文言 1
WENYAN-02-01.original: 坤至柔而動也剛，至靜而德方。後得主而有常，含萬物而化光。坤道其順乎！承天而時行。
WENYAN-02-01.essay: Kun is supremely yielding, yet its movement can be strong; it is supremely still, yet its character remains upright and firmly shaped. These qualities are not contradictions. Receptivity allows Kun to support the initiating activity represented by Qian and to carry things through to completion. By following the appropriate lead, it keeps to a reliable pattern, embraces the many forms of life, and enables them to flourish. Its distinctive power lies in receiving, nurturing, and acting at the proper time. The passage praises responsiveness as an active virtue rather than simple passivity.

WENYAN-02-02.label: 02 坤 文言 2
WENYAN-02-02.original: 積善之家，必有餘慶；積不善之家，必有餘殃。臣弒其君，子弒其父，非一朝一夕之故，其所由來者漸矣。由辨之不早辨也。易曰：「履霜，堅冰至。」蓋言順也。
WENYAN-02-02.essay: A family that steadily accumulates good conduct may leave benefits to later generations, just as persistent wrongdoing can produce harm. The text illustrates this cumulative process with the grave examples of a minister killing his ruler and a son killing his father. Such events do not arise overnight; they are preceded by small developments that were not recognized or corrected early enough. 'Treading on frost; hard ice will come' summarizes this principle. The passage urges attention to early signs because repeated choices can gradually establish a direction that becomes difficult to reverse.

WENYAN-02-03.label: 02 坤 文言 3
WENYAN-02-03.original: 直其正也，方其義也。君子敬以直內，義以方外，敬義立而德不孤。「直方大，不習无不利。」則不疑其所行也。
WENYAN-02-03.essay: Straightness refers to inner rectitude, while squareness describes outward conduct shaped by what is right. A cultivated person establishes the inner life through respect and care, then gives external behavior a reliable form through justice. When reverence and righteousness work together, good character is not isolated from action or from other people. The description of being straight, square, and great therefore concerns more than a set of abstract virtues. It portrays someone whose convictions, decisions, and outward behavior fit together so consistently that action need not be accompanied by uncertainty.

WENYAN-02-04.label: 02 坤 文言 4
WENYAN-02-04.original: 陰雖有美，含之。以從王事，弗敢成也。地道也，妻道也，臣道也。地道无成，而代有終也。
WENYAN-02-04.essay: Even when receptive strength possesses fine qualities, it may keep them inward rather than display them. In service to the ruler, it helps a larger undertaking reach completion without claiming all the credit. The original passage presents this through the traditional roles of earth, wife, and minister, each understood as assisting a larger process. These are descriptions of a historical model of complementary functions, not a requirement that modern people accept its social hierarchy. Within that framework, Kun's virtue is to support successful completion without insisting on personal prominence.

WENYAN-02-05.label: 02 坤 文言 5
WENYAN-02-05.original: 天地變化，草木蕃；天地閉，賢人隱。易曰：「括囊，无咎，无譽。」蓋言謹也。
WENYAN-02-05.essay: When heaven and earth interact, plants and trees flourish; when that interaction closes, worthy people may withdraw from public life. The saying about closing a bag's opening describes caution at a time when open action would be unwise. It promises neither applause nor a spectacular achievement: it speaks of avoiding blame even if no reputation is gained. The commentary links restraint to the conditions of the age. A thoughtful person may need to protect integrity by speaking less and declining involvement until circumstances become more favorable.

WENYAN-02-06.label: 02 坤 文言 6
WENYAN-02-06.original: 君子黃中通理，正位居體，美在其中，而暢於四支，發於事業，美之至也。
WENYAN-02-06.essay: Yellow symbolizes balance at the center. The cultivated person is inwardly centered, understands principles clearly, and occupies a fitting position. Goodness is not confined to thought: it becomes visible in bodily conduct and then in public work. The passage moves from inner qualities to outward expression, showing how coherent character affects what a person does. This is called the highest form of beauty because personal values and practical deeds are not separated. The imagery belongs to the traditional symbolism of Kun, where inward steadiness supports effective action.

WENYAN-02-07.label: 02 坤 文言 7
WENYAN-02-07.original: 陰疑於陽必戰，為其嫌於无陽也，故稱龍焉。猶未離其類也，故稱血焉。夫玄黃者，天地之雜也。天玄而地黃。
WENYAN-02-07.essay: When yin becomes so powerful that it rivals yang, conflict emerges. The commentary explains why the related line speaks of dragons and blood: the dragon acknowledges the opposing yang force, while blood indicates that yin has not ceased to belong to its own kind. The mingling colors, dark and yellow, symbolize heaven and earth interwoven in the struggle. The passage is a traditional account of complementary forces becoming antagonistic when balance is lost. It describes the imagery of a dangerous extreme rather than celebrating the conflict itself.

XICI-U-01-01.label: 第一章 第 1 段
XICI-U-01-01.original: 天尊地卑，乾坤定矣。卑高以陳，貴賤位矣。動靜有常，剛柔斷矣。方以類聚，物以羣分，吉凶生矣。在天成象，在地成形，變化見矣。是故剛柔相摩，八卦相荡，鼓之以雷霆，潤之以風雨，日月運行，一寒一暑。乾道成男，坤道成女；乾知大始，坤作成物；乾以易知，坤以簡能；易則易知，簡則易從；易知則有親，易從則有功；有親則可久，有功則可大；可久則賢人之德，可大則賢人之業。易簡，而天下之理得矣。天下之理得，而成位乎其中矣。
XICI-U-01-01.essay: The passage begins with heaven above and earth below as a way of describing the distinct but related roles of Qian and Kun. Movement and stillness, strength and yielding, and the grouping of things by kind make differences and change visible. Thunder, rain, wind, sunlight, and the alternating seasons give concrete examples. Qian is associated with initiating life, while Kun brings things into form. The author then emphasizes ease and simplicity: what is clear can be understood and trusted, and what is straightforward can be practiced effectively. Understanding these principles allows people to find their place within the larger order of heaven and earth.

XICI-U-02-01.label: 第二章 第 1 段
XICI-U-02-01.original: 聖人設卦觀象，繫辭焉而明吉凶；剛柔相推而生變化。是故吉凶者，失得之象也。悔吝者，憂虞之象也。變化者，進退之象也。剛柔者，晝夜之象也。六爻之動，三極之道也。是故君子所居而安者，易之序也。所樂而玩者，爻之辭也。是故君子居則觀其象而玩其辭，動則觀其變而玩其占；是以自天祐之，吉无不利。
XICI-U-02-01.essay: The sages established hexagrams by observing images and added statements to distinguish favorable and unfavorable situations. As firm and yielding lines interact, circumstances change. Good fortune and misfortune describe gain and loss; regret and difficulty warn of emerging problems; advance and retreat are different expressions of change. The six lines connect patterns associated with heaven, earth, and human life. A thoughtful person studies the arrangement of the Changes in quiet times and attends to the words attached to each line. When action is required, the person also considers changing lines and divination, seeking a responsible response rather than treating one judgment as unchangeable.

XICI-U-03-01.label: 第三章 第 1 段
XICI-U-03-01.original: 彖者，言乎象者也。爻者，言乎變者也。吉凶者，言乎其失得也。悔吝者，言乎其小疵也。无咎者，善補過也。是故列貴賤者存乎位，齊小大者存乎卦，辯吉凶者存乎辭，憂悔吝者存乎介，震无咎者存乎悔。是故卦有小大，辭有險易，辭也者，各指其所之。
XICI-U-03-01.essay: This passage explains the different functions of the text. The judgment on a hexagram describes its overall image, while individual lines show movement and changing conditions. Good or bad fortune concerns possible gains and losses; regret and difficulty point to smaller faults or warning signs. “No blame” does not mean that mistakes never happen: it means that errors can be recognized and repaired appropriately. Positions distinguish higher and lower roles, while the hexagram as a whole shows the scale of the situation. Its words may sound reassuring or dangerous because they point toward different possible outcomes. Interpretation must therefore consider position, context, and the direction of change together.

XICI-U-04-01.label: 第四章 第 1 段
XICI-U-04-01.original: 易與天地準，故能彌綸天地之道。仰以觀於天文，俯以察於地理，是故知幽明之故。原始反終，故知死生之說。精氣為物，遊魂為變，是故知鬼神之情狀。與天地相似，故不違；知周乎萬物，而道濟天下，故不過；旁行而不流，樂天知命，故不憂；安土敦乎仁，故能愛；範圍天地之化而不過，曲成萬物而不遺，通乎晝夜之道而知，故神无方而易无體。
XICI-U-04-01.essay: The Changes is presented as a way of understanding patterns in heaven, earth, and human existence. Looking upward to celestial phenomena and downward to the terrain reveals both visible and hidden processes. Reflecting on beginnings and endings encourages thought about life and death; references to vital energy, wandering spirits, and divine beings reflect the ancient intellectual world of the text. Its ideal is not to withdraw from people but to understand many things without excess, act with compassion, and remain at ease with one's circumstances. Change has no single permanent shape: like day becoming night, its operations must be recognized through the particular situation rather than reduced to one fixed formula.

XICI-U-05-01.label: 第五章 第 1 段
XICI-U-05-01.original: 一陰一陽之謂道：繼之者善也，成之者性也；仁者見之謂之仁，知者見之謂之知；百姓日用而不知，故君子之道鮮矣。顯諸仁，藏諸用，鼓萬物而不與聖人同憂，盛德大業至矣哉！富有之謂大業，日新之謂盛德，生生之謂易，成象之謂乾，效法之謂坤，極數知來之謂占，通變之謂事，陰陽不測之謂神。
XICI-U-05-01.essay: The familiar expression “one yin and one yang is called the Way” describes reality as an ongoing relationship between complementary forces. What carries this movement forward is called goodness, and what becomes established within living beings is called their nature. Different observers may recognize compassion or wisdom in the same process, while everyday users may not notice it at all. The passage links great achievement with abundance and great virtue with continual renewal. “Change” means life generating more life. Qian forms initiating images; Kun follows and completes them. Divination explores what may come, practical affairs require adaptability, and the mysterious character of yin and yang is described as spirit.

XICI-U-06-01.label: 第六章 第 1 段
XICI-U-06-01.original: 夫易，廣矣！大矣！以言乎遠則不禦，以言乎邇則靜而正，以言乎天地之間則備矣！夫乾，其靜也專，其動也直，是以大生焉。夫坤，其靜也翕，其動也闢，是以廣生焉。廣大配天地，變通配四時，陰陽之義配日月，易簡之善配至德。
XICI-U-06-01.essay: The Changes is called vast because its patterns apply both to remote and nearby things. Considered on a grand scale, it reaches beyond any obvious boundary; considered closely, it can be quiet, precise, and orderly. Qian is described as concentrated when still and direct when active, the source of great beginnings. Kun gathers when still and opens when active, giving wide scope for things to develop. These two qualities complement each other rather than compete. The text compares their breadth to heaven and earth, their adaptability to the seasons, and yin and yang to the sun and moon. Ease and simplicity are treated as expressions of exceptional virtue.

XICI-U-07-01.label: 第七章 第 1 段
XICI-U-07-01.original: 子曰：「易其至矣乎！夫易，聖人所以崇德而廣業也，知崇禮卑，崇效天，卑法地。天地設位，而易行乎其中矣。成性存存，道義之門。」
XICI-U-07-01.essay: Confucius is quoted as praising the Changes as a profound resource for cultivating character and enlarging worthy undertakings. Wisdom should aspire upward, like heaven, while proper conduct should remain humble, like earth. The point is not to choose intellect over courtesy or humility over achievement. A mature person needs both: expansive understanding and grounded behavior. Heaven and earth each have their position, and the movement of change unfolds between them. By repeatedly preserving and refining one's own moral nature, a person enters the path of duty and right conduct. The passage thus approaches the Changes as a guide to ethical development, not merely a collection of predictions.

XICI-U-08-01.label: 第八章 第 1 段
XICI-U-08-01.original: 聖人有以見天下之賾，而擬諸其形容，象其物宜，是故謂之象。聖人有以見天下之動，而觀其會通，以行其典禮，繫辭焉以斷其吉凶，是故謂之爻。言天下之至賾而不可惡也，言天下之至動而不可亂也。擬之而後言，議之而後動，擬議以成其變化。
XICI-U-08-01.essay: The sages perceived complexities in the world and fashioned images resembling the appropriate features of things. Such images became the symbolic language of the Changes. They also observed movement, relationships, and recurring patterns; the lines and their statements describe these developments and distinguish favorable from unfavorable directions. The text claims that even difficult realities can be represented without becoming impossible to understand, and constant movement can be discussed without losing order. Its closing advice is practical: compare and examine a situation before speaking, and deliberate before acting. Careful interpretation and discussion help people respond to change instead of reacting to appearances alone.

XICI-U-08-02.label: 第八章 第 2 段
XICI-U-08-02.original: 「鳴鶴在陰，其子和之。我有好爵，吾與爾靡之。」子曰：「君子居其室，出其言善，則千里之外應之，況其邇者乎！居其室，出其言不善，則千里之外違之，況其邇者乎！言出乎身加乎民；行發乎邇見乎遠。言行，君子之樞機；樞機之發，榮辱之主也。言行，君子之所以動天地也，可不慎乎！」「同人，先號咷而後笑。」子曰：「君子之道，或出或處，或默或語。二人同心，其利斷金。同心之言，其臭如蘭。」
XICI-U-08-02.essay: A crane calling from a hidden place is answered by its young, suggesting that genuine words can be heard far beyond their source. The passage explains that good speech may inspire people even a thousand miles away, while harmful speech can drive them away. Words and actions are a pivot on which honor and disgrace turn, so they demand care. The second quotation, from Fellowship with Others, moves from crying to laughter. People may serve or withdraw, speak or remain silent, yet two people who truly share one purpose can overcome formidable obstacles. Their agreement is likened to a fragrance as pleasing as orchids.

XICI-U-08-03.label: 第八章 第 3 段
XICI-U-08-03.original: 「初六，藉用白茅，无咎。」子曰：「苟錯諸地而可矣。藉之用茅，何咎之有！慎之至也。夫茅之為物薄而用可重也，慎斯術也以往，其无所失矣。」
XICI-U-08-03.essay: The line about placing an offering on white thatch illustrates exceptional care. An offering could simply be set on the ground, yet placing a thin layer of clean grass beneath it shows additional respect. The grass itself is ordinary and inexpensive, but its use in the right setting carries weight. The lesson is not that elaborate ceremony is always necessary. Rather, attention to a small detail can reveal the seriousness with which an important duty is undertaken. If this attitude of thoughtful preparation is extended to other activities, unnecessary errors become less likely. The text connects prudence in a simple ritual act with steadiness in broader conduct.

XICI-U-08-04.label: 第八章 第 4 段
XICI-U-08-04.original: 「勞謙，君子有終，吉。」子曰：「勞而不伐，有功而不德，厚之至也；語以其功下人者也。德言盛，禮言恭；謙也者，致恭以存其位者也。」
XICI-U-08-04.essay: The passage interprets the line about a hardworking yet modest person who reaches a good conclusion. Such a person has accomplishments but does not advertise them, and contributes without claiming every result as personal merit. The text calls this depth of character. Virtue concerns the fullness of one's inner qualities, while ritual propriety concerns the respectful manner in which those qualities are expressed. Modesty does not erase achievement; it prevents success from turning into arrogance. Someone who can lower themselves in relation to others despite real accomplishments is better able to preserve trust and standing. The line therefore links sustained success with humility rather than display.

XICI-U-08-05.label: 第八章 第 5 段
XICI-U-08-05.original: 「亢龍有悔。」子曰：「貴而无位，高而无民，賢人在下位而无輔，是以動而有悔也。」
XICI-U-08-05.essay: The expression “a dragon that rises too high has cause for regret” is explained through the isolation of an exalted person. Someone may appear powerful yet lack a secure role, stand above others without public support, and fail to receive help from capable people below. Height alone is not effective leadership. When a person is cut off from colleagues, advisers, and those affected by decisions, even a seemingly strong position becomes unstable. Acting forcefully under such conditions is likely to bring regret. The image of the overreaching dragon warns about the danger of success carried beyond its proper limits, not about ambition in every circumstance.

XICI-U-08-06.label: 第八章 第 6 段
XICI-U-08-06.original: 「不出戶庭，无咎。」子曰：「亂之所生也，則言語以為階。君不密則失臣，臣不密則失身，幾事不密則害成；是以君子慎密而不出也。」
XICI-U-08-06.essay: The advice not to step beyond the inner courtyard is connected here with discretion in speech. Disorder often begins when words disclose matters that should have remained confidential. If a ruler cannot keep confidence, ministers may be lost; if a minister is indiscreet, personal safety may be endangered; if sensitive plans leak too early, a valuable undertaking may fail. The passage does not praise silence in every situation. It distinguishes the right time to speak from situations requiring careful restraint. A cultivated person weighs responsibility, audience, and timing before sharing information. Guarding words becomes part of preserving trust and enabling important work to reach completion.

XICI-U-08-07.label: 第八章 第 7 段
XICI-U-08-07.original: 子曰：「作易者，其知盜乎！易曰：『負且乘，致寇至。』負也者，小人之事也。乘也者，君子之器也。小人而乘君子之器，盜思奪之矣。上慢下暴，盜思伐之矣。慢藏誨盜，冶容誨淫。易曰：『負且乘，致寇至。』盜之招也。」
XICI-U-08-07.essay: This passage uses the image of someone carrying a burden while riding a distinguished carriage to discuss social roles and the attraction of thieves. In its ancient hierarchy, a carriage could signal status that the rider had not earned, inviting others to seize it. Arrogance above and aggression below can likewise provoke conflict. The text adds that careless storage attracts theft and ostentatious display invites improper attention. These claims reflect historical moral assumptions and should not be taken as excuses for wrongdoing. The central interpretive point is that visible behavior, mismatched responsibilities, and neglected precautions can create avoidable risks. The Changes asks readers to examine the conditions surrounding trouble.

XICI-U-09-01.label: 第九章 第 1 段
XICI-U-09-01.original: 天一地二，天三地四，天五地六，天七地八，天九地十。天數五，地數五，五位相得而各有合。天數二十有五，地數三十，凡天地之數，五十有五，此所以成變化，而行鬼神也。大衍之數五十，其用四十有九，分而為二以象兩，掛一以象三，揲之以四以象四時，歸奇於扐以象閏，五歲再閏，故再扐而後掛。
XICI-U-09-01.essay: The passage lays out an ancient numerical account of divination. Odd numbers one, three, five, seven, and nine belong to heaven and total twenty-five; even numbers two, four, six, eight, and ten belong to earth and total thirty. Together they make fifty-five. In the great expansion method, fifty yarrow stalks are counted but forty-nine are used. They are divided into two groups to symbolize the two primary powers; one stalk is set aside to represent a third element. Counting in fours evokes the four seasons, and the remainders evoke intercalary months. These are symbolic procedures within the classical divination system, not a description of modern probability theory.

XICI-U-09-02.label: 第九章 第 2 段
XICI-U-09-02.original: 乾之策，二百一十有六，坤之策，百四十有四，凡三百有六十，當期之日。二篇之策，萬有一千五百二十，當萬物之數也。是故四營而成易，十有八變而成卦，八卦而小成；引而伸之，觸類而長之，天下之能事畢矣。顯道神德行，是故可與酬酢，可與祐神矣。子曰：「知變化之道者，其知神之所為乎！」
XICI-U-09-02.essay: Here the text calculates the number of yarrow-stalk values associated with Qian and Kun. Qian's six lines amount to 216, and Kun's to 144, making 360, a number compared with the days of a traditional year. Across the two parts of the Changes, the total is given as 11,520, symbolically associated with the multitude of things. Four operations complete a change, and eighteen changes produce a hexagram. From the eight foundational trigrams, the method can be extended to many combinations and situations. The author treats numerical procedures as a disciplined way to disclose patterns of transformation, while the invocation of spirits belongs to its ancient worldview.

XICI-U-10-01.label: 第十章 第 1 段
XICI-U-10-01.original: 易有聖人之道四焉：以言者尚其辭，以動者尚其變，以制器者尚其象，以卜筮者尚其占。是以君子將有為也，將有行也，問焉而以言，其受命也如響，无有遠近幽深，遂知來物。非天下之至精，其孰能與於此！
XICI-U-10-01.essay: The text identifies four ways the sages use the Changes. For speech and interpretation, they value its written statements; for action, they attend to transformation; for designing objects, they study images; and for divination, they consider the resulting judgments. A cultivated person who faces a decision can consult the system as though asking a question and receiving an answering echo. Its traditional description emphasizes that distance or obscurity need not prevent a meaningful response. This is a claim within the classical theory of divination, not proof that every future event can be predicted. The broader lesson is that words, images, changing circumstances, and practical choices serve distinct but connected roles.

XICI-U-10-02.label: 第十章 第 2 段
XICI-U-10-02.original: 參伍以變，錯綜其數，通其變，遂成天下之文，極其數，遂定天下之象；非天下之至變，其孰能與於此！
XICI-U-10-02.essay: The passage describes combining and recombining numbers to perceive transformation. By comparing patterns and arranging them in different relationships, the diviner seeks the structures that make phenomena intelligible. Extending numerical operations to their limits is said to establish the images through which the world can be represented. The text admires the ability of the Changes to hold variation and structure together: the combinations are not arbitrary figures but part of an ordered symbolic system. It calls this extraordinary adaptability. In reading the passage, it is useful to distinguish its historical philosophical claim about numerical symbolism from a modern scientific claim about the causes of events.

XICI-U-10-03.label: 第十章 第 3 段
XICI-U-10-03.original: 易，无思也，无為也，寂然不動，感而遂通天下之故。非天下之至神，其孰能與於此！
XICI-U-10-03.essay: The Changes is described as having neither private thoughts nor deliberate actions. It remains still and silent, yet when approached through its method, it is said to respond and disclose the underlying reasons for things. The emphasis is on the contrast between inactivity and meaningful response. Unlike a human adviser, the classic is not imagined as pursuing interests or making choices of its own. In the traditional account, its symbolic arrangement becomes informative through the encounter between a question and a changing pattern. The author calls this mysterious, even divine. Readers can understand the passage as expressing the perceived depth of divination without treating the claim as an established physical mechanism.

XICI-U-10-04.label: 第十章 第 4 段
XICI-U-10-04.original: 夫易，聖人之所以極深而研幾也！唯深也，故能通天下之志；唯幾也，故能成天下之務；唯神也，故不疾而速，不行而至。
XICI-U-10-04.essay: The Changes is portrayed as a means by which sages investigate both the deepest principles and the first, almost invisible signs of events. Because their inquiry reaches deeply, they can understand people's intentions; because they notice early indications, they can address difficult affairs before they grow. Its work is described as so subtle that it seems to act quickly without haste and arrive without travel. These striking phrases celebrate insight into connected processes, not literal movement across space. The passage joins patient study with timely action. It suggests that a decision becomes more effective when one understands broad conditions and recognizes small changes before they become obvious.

XICI-U-10-05.label: 第十章 第 5 段
XICI-U-10-05.original: 子曰「易有聖人之道四焉」者，此之謂也。
